citation.title: Convolutional Neural Network-based Topology Optimization (CNN-TO) By Estimating Sensitivity of Compliance from Material Distribution
citation.authors: Yusuke Takahashi, Yoshiro Suzuki, Akira Todoroki
citation.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.LG; also cs.CE); p. 1 says the paper is under review at the ASME Journal of Computing and Information Science in Engineering; no version of record found (web search 2026-09-24)
citation.version_coded: arXiv v1 (23 Dec 2019; only version), PDF

included.reason: I-SPEED (screened I-QUALITY; the first quantitative classical comparison in the full text is a computation-time comparison, §5.1 rule 2)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: For 40 density updates on a 16×32 cantilever, CNN-TO took 33.5 s on a Xeon PC with four GPUs, versus 7.28 s for FEM-based SIMP on a 1.60 GHz Core i5 PC; the ML method is about 4.6× slower [derived].
claim.key_phrase: the proposed method requires more computation time than the previous method
claim.location: Sec. 5.2.1 and Table 2, p. 7 (first quantitative comparison with the classical method; the abstract, conclusion and introduction are qualitative, so §5.1 rule 2 applies)
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Derived: 7.28 s (SIMP, 40 updates) ÷ 33.5 s (CNN-TO, 40 updates) = 0.217 (Table 2), i.e. CNN-TO is about 4.6× slower; per update 0.182 s vs 0.84 s [derived]. Different machines: SIMP on a Core i5-4500U PC without GPU, CNN-TO on a Xeon Silver 4112 PC with 4× GTX 1080 Ti (Sec. 4).
claim.alternatives: (1) Quality, Table 3 (the result behind the abstract's claim of a little higher performance [inferred]): dimensionless compliance 1,287 (CNN-TO) vs 1,294 (SIMP), initial design 5,974; 0.54% lower [derived]. (2) Speed proxy, qualitative (conclusion; Sec. 5.2.1, 5.3.3; Figs. 12-13): CNN-TO reaches the structure outline in fewer updates (outline after 5 updates). (3) Qualitative (abstract, conclusion; Sec. 5.2.2): CNN-TO finds a topology that SIMP from random starts did not find; Appendix 2 shows that SIMP restarted from the CNN-TO design barely changes it.

baseline.classical_method: SIMP compliance minimization (p = 3, volume limit 50%) with optimality-criteria updates from FEM sensitivities, uniform initial density, followed by threshold filtering and floating-island removal (Sec. 2.2-2.4, 4)
baseline.implementation: not stated for SIMP specifically; the article lists Python with TensorFlow for the CNN and NumPy/SciPy for other calculations (Sec. 4) [SIMP inferred to use NumPy/SciPy]
baseline.hardware_classical: PC with 8 GB RAM and an Intel Core i5-4500U @ 1.60 GHz, no GPU (Sec. 4)
baseline.hardware_ml: 128 GB PC with an Intel Xeon Silver 4112 @ 2.60 GHz; CNN run in parallel on 4× NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti (Sec. 4)
baseline.classical_iterations: fixed 40 density updates for both methods in the comparison (Table 2; Fig. 11 caption); Sec. 2.4 describes a change-based stopping rule whose threshold is not stated
baseline.training_time: not stated (Adam, learning rate 0.00005; two CNNs trained from different initial weights, Sec. 4, 5.3.2)
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated; training data are random bar-system structures with FEM-computed sensitivities; sample count not stated (Sec. 3.2.1-3.2.2)
baseline.quality_metric: dimensionless compliance of the filtered final designs (Table 3); compliance histories (Fig. 13); visual comparison (Figs. 11-12, 14)
baseline.quality_gap: 1,287 (CNN-TO) vs 1,294 (SIMP) after different filters, initial design 5,974 (Table 3); 0.54% lower [derived]; final volumes not reported

R1.evidence: Table 2 and Sec. 5.2.1: both methods are timed for the same 40 density updates, and the filtered final compliances are nearly equal (1,294 vs 1,287, Table 3). Matching is not exact: different post-processing filters (Appendix 1), a SIMP threshold set only to give a volume close to CNN-TO's (Sec. 2.3), unreported final volumes, and no statement on whether filtering time is in Table 2. Unsure, so pass; a stricter reading gives partial (R1-loose).

R2.evidence: Sec. 4: SIMP ran on a PC with a Core i5-4500U @ 1.60 GHz and 8 GB RAM, without GPU; CNN-TO ran on a 128 GB Xeon Silver 4112 PC with four GTX 1080 Ti GPUs; the choice is not justified. SIMP needs 0.182 s per update at 16×32 [derived: 7.28 s ÷ 40], which suggests an unoptimized implementation (NumPy/SciPy [inferred]; solver not stated); this is an R2(e) candidate that needs our per-iteration timing at this size. (c) does not apply (about 1.1×10³ DOFs [derived]); (b) and (d) are not established. The asymmetry penalizes the classical side, so it cannot explain the ML method's slower time.

R3.evidence: Sec. 3.2.1-3.2.2 and 4: neither the CNN training time nor the cost of generating the bar-system training structures and their FEM sensitivities is reported (sample count not stated), and no break-even is given; Table 2 covers only the 40 updates. The omission favours the ML side, which is still slower.

R4.evidence: Table 3 and Fig. 11: the compliance of the filtered final designs is reported for both methods (FE analysis [inferred]). Final volumes are not reported, although the authors note that hole filling can break the mass constraint (Sec. 3.2.4). Raw CNN-TO outputs contain disconnected parts that the filter removes (Fig. 7). One example only; no failure count.

reporting.n_test_cases: 1 problem (16×32 cantilever); CNN-TO repeated with two CNNs trained from different initial weights (Fig. 14) and several runs with one CNN (Appendix 3, Fig. 17); SIMP run from random initial designs more than once, results not tabulated (Sec. 5.2.2)

notes: Primary-outcome choice is a judgment call. Read strictly, §5.1 rule 2 selects the first quantitative classical comparison in the main text, Table 2 (time, ML slower), which gives stratum speed with direction underperform. The screening code (I-QUALITY) and the abstract's emphasis point to Table 3 (compliance 1,287 vs 1,294); under §5.1 rule 4 a verifier may pick that instead, which gives stratum Q with R3 = na. The conclusion's claim of fewer update steps is a speed proxy shown only graphically (Figs. 12-13); CNN-TO would need fewer than about 8.7 updates to match SIMP's 40-update time [derived: 7.28 s ÷ 0.8375 s per update], and no time-to-quality comparison is reported. The hardware asymmetry favours the ML side, which is still slower. The FEM settings print Poisson's ratio ν = 1.0 (Sec. 4), which is not admissible for isotropic plane elasticity [inferred; likely a typo]. The two methods use different post-processing filters (Appendix 1). seeds_or_variance = yes: Sec. 5.3.2 shows that two training seeds give different optima (qualitative only; no compliance given for CNN 2). The Appendix 3 text cites Fig. 16 where Fig. 17 is meant. No code or data statement. retest_candidate false: no public code. The problem is tiny (16×32) and fully specified, so a baseline-only R2(e) check of the 0.182 s per-update SIMP time is possible once our strong baseline is timed at this size. Reporting locators: hardware and timing = Sec. 4 and Table 2; n = Sec. 4, 5.3.2 and Appendix 3.
